target: Wir dürfen im Naturschutzgebiet keine Pflanzen pflücken.
english: We may not pick plants in the nature reserve.
old: 'Dürfen' with 'nicht' expresses prohibition – 'not allowed to'.
focus: Negated dürfen = forbidden, not 'don't have to' – anchor in 'dürfen ... keine Pflanzen pflücken' (the card uses keine, not nicht) and keep it to that one rule.

target: Die Bewerbungen werden von der Personalabteilung sorgfältig geprüft.
english: The applications are carefully reviewed by the HR department.
old: 'von' + dative marks the agent in passive sentences.
focus: 'by' in a passive is von, not bei – quote 'von der Personalabteilung geprüft'; bei would mean 'at'. Say 'the doer' in plain words, not 'the agent'.

target: Das Bild hängt an der Wand über dem Sofa.
english: The picture hangs on the wall above the sofa.
old: 'An' + dative: location – 'an der Wand' (position).
focus: Two-way preposition: static location takes dative – 'an der Wand' (the picture just hangs there); movement toward would flip it to accusative. Add that contrast as the hook.

target: Sie hätte das Konzert gern besucht, aber die Karten waren ausverkauft.
english: She would have liked to attend the concert, but the tickets were sold out.
old: 'hätte' – konjunktiv II of haben (hat), softening this into a hypothetical or polite expression.
focus: 'hätte ... gern besucht' = 'would have liked to attend' – counterfactual past, not softening/politeness as the current tip claims. Anchor in the card's own phrase.

target: Ein kalter Wind weht von Norden.
english: A cold wind blows from the north.
old: After 'ein': adj. takes '-er' (nom. masculine).
focus: With 'ein' showing no gender, the adjective takes over the job: 'ein kalter Wind' – kalter carries the -er that der would have shown. Quote 'kalter', drop the abbreviations (adj., nom.).

target: Sie sagte, sie wolle nächstes Jahr nach Kanada auswandern.
english: She said she wanted to emigrate to Canada next year.
old: 'habe' + Partizip II = Konj. I perfect in reported speech.
focus: The card shows 'wolle' – Konjunktiv I marks reported speech ('she said she wanted to'). Drop the current 'habe + Partizip II' claim, which does not occur in this sentence; anchor in wolle.

target: Das ist nicht mein Koffer, meiner ist schwarz.
english: That is not my suitcase, mine is black.
old: 'Nicht' before possessives negates the whole predicate: 'nicht mein Koffer'.
focus: German negates a possessive noun with 'nicht', never 'kein': 'nicht mein Koffer' (kein is only for article-less nouns).

target: Hallo, ich freue mich sehr.
english: Hello, I'm very happy to see you.
old: 'Sich freuen' is a reflexive verb meaning 'to be happy/pleased'.
focus: German makes 'happy' reflexive: 'ich freue mich' (lit. I gladden myself) where English has no reflexive.

target: Heute ist es kälter als gestern.
english: Today is colder than yesterday.
old: Inversion required: if anything other than the subject opens a sentence, swap the verb and subject. `Morgen kommt er` – never `Morgen er kommt`.
focus: V2 inversion, quote THIS card: 'Heute ist es kälter' puts the verb before the subject 'es' because Heute opens the clause. Strip backticks.

target: Wir wissen nicht, ob das Geschäft sonntags geöffnet ist.
english: We don't know whether the shop is open on Sundays.
old: 'Ob' (whether) creates indirect yes/no questions with verb-final order: 'Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt'.
focus: ob = 'whether' and pushes the verb to the end; quote THIS card: 'ob das Geschäft sonntags geöffnet ist'.

target: Schalten Sie bitte Ihre Mobiltelefone auf lautlos.
english: Please switch your mobile phones to silent.
old: Formal imperative keeps 'Sie' after the verb: 'Kommen Sie!' The 'wir' form means 'let's': 'Gehen wir!'
focus: One rule only: formal imperative keeps Sie right after the verb, same order as a question. Quote 'Schalten Sie...'; drop the wir='let's' clause.

target: Er spricht fließender Deutsch als seine Mitschüler.
english: He speaks German more fluently than his classmates.
old: 'Als' is used for comparisons (bigger than): 'größer als'. Don't confuse with 'wie' which is used for equality: 'so groß wie'.
focus: als = 'than' for comparisons: 'fließender als'; wie = 'as...as' for equality. Quote the card's 'fließender als', don't use größer.

target: Wir verstehen uns trotz unserer Unterschiede sehr gut.
english: We get along very well despite our differences.
old: 'Sich verstehen' – reciprocal: 'to get along with each other'.
focus: Reflexive 'sich verstehen' = 'get along', not 'understand': 'wir verstehen uns gut'.

target: Sag Bescheid, falls du Hilfe beim Streichen der Wohnung brauchst.
english: Let me know if you need help painting the apartment.
old: 'Sag!' – du-imperative, formed by dropping -st. Strong verbs with e→i keep the change (gib!, nimm!).
focus: du-imperative = verb stem minus -st, no 'du': 'Sag Bescheid' (not 'du sagst'). One rule; drop the strong-verb clause.

target: Ich halte es für äußerst wichtig, dass Kinder schon früh Fremdsprachen lernen.
english: I consider it extremely important that children learn foreign languages early.
old: 'Ich halte es für' + adj. = formal way to state opinion.
focus: 'halten für' = consider/regard as (lit. 'hold for'): 'ich halte es für wichtig' = I consider it important. Drop the 'formal' framing.

target: Ich spreche über meine Pläne.
english: I talk about my plans.
old: 'Über' + accusative for topic.
focus: uber = 'about' a topic and takes the accusative; quote 'uber meine Plane'; plain words, no motion here just topic.

target: Ich habe Angst vor Spinnen.
english: I am afraid of spiders.
old: 'Angst haben vor' + dative.
focus: Fear rides a fixed frame: Angst haben vor + dative; quote 'Angst vor Spinnen'.

target: Guten Morgen! Ich hätte gern ein weiches Brötchen.
english: Good morning! I'd like a soft bread roll.
old: 'Guten Morgen' – accusative in a greeting: 'ein guter Morgen' → '(ich wünsche) einen guten Morgen'.
focus: Lead with the surprise: a German greeting is leftover '(ich wunsche) einen guten Morgen', so it is accusative; quote 'Guten Morgen'; drop the 'accusative' lead.

target: Wir haben uns gefreut, als wir die gute Nachricht erhalten haben.
english: We were happy when we received the good news.
old: 'Als' (when, for single past events) is subordinating – verb goes to the end: 'Als ich Kind war, ...'
focus: als = when for a single completed past event (vs wenn for repeated); quote card's 'als wir die gute Nachricht erhalten haben' with the verb at the end; drop the off-card example.

target: Räum dein Zimmer auf, bevor du dich mit Freunden triffst.
english: Tidy your room before you meet with friends.
old: German reflexive: pronouns mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich. `Ich freue mich` = 'I'm happy / I look forward to'. The `mich` is mandatory – without it the verb means something else.
focus: Reflexive dich is mandatory with sich treffen; strip backticks; quote 'du dich mit Freunden triffst'; without dich the verb means something else.

target: Die Lehrerin, deren Unterricht mir am besten gefällt, unterrichtet Biologie.
english: The teacher whose lessons I like best teaches biology.
old: 'deren' (gen. fem./pl.) introduces a relative clause – its case depends on its role within that clause.
focus: deren = 'whose' (a genitive relative word); quote 'deren Unterricht'; plain words, drop 'gen. fem./pl.'

target: Schön, dass du kommen konntest!
english: Nice that you could come!
old: In 'dass' clauses, the conjugated verb moves to the very end: 'Ich weiß, dass er morgen kommt'.
focus: Anchor to the card: in a dass-clause the verb goes last; quote 'dass du kommen konntest' (konntest at the end).

target: Wir gehen spazieren, obwohl es draußen regnet.
english: We go for a walk although it is raining outside.
old: 'Obwohl' (although) – verb final: '... es draußen regnet'.
focus: Add the hook: unlike English, obwohl pushes the verb to the very end; quote 'obwohl es draussen regnet'.

target: In diesem Restaurant wird das Essen frisch zubereitet.
english: In this restaurant, the food is prepared fresh.
old: Present passive: 'wird' + Partizip II.
focus: German passive uses werden (become), not sein; quote 'wird ... zubereitet'; avoid 'Partizip II' jargon. Keep as the single passive tip.

target: Wegen des Staus bin ich eine Stunde zu spät gekommen.
english: Because of the traffic jam I arrived an hour late.
old: 'Wegen' + genitive – 'wegen des Staus'.
focus: wegen + genitive = 'because of'; quote 'wegen des Staus'; note spoken German often slips to dative. Representative genitive-preposition tip.

target: Der Zug, auf den wir warten, hat zwanzig Minuten Verspätung.
english: The train we are waiting for has a twenty-minute delay.
old: Relative pronoun: 'auf den' – accusative after 'warten auf'.
focus: warten auf takes accusative, so the relative pronoun is 'auf den' not 'auf dem' — the preposition sets the case

target: Der Brief ist geschrieben worden.
english: The letter has been written.
old: Passive perfect: 'sein' + participle + 'worden'.
focus: perfect passive uses bare 'worden' not 'geworden' — 'ist geschrieben worden' = has been written

target: Er behauptet, er habe das Geld bereits überwiesen.
english: He claims he already transferred the money.
old: Recipes traditionally use Konjunktiv I: 'Man nehme 200g Mehl' (One takes 200g flour) – though this is becoming rare.
focus: 'er habe' is Konjunktiv I for reported speech — flags this as his claim, the speaker not vouching for it

target: Ich wünschte, ich könnte besser singen.
english: I wish I could sing better.
old: 'Wünschte' + Konjunktiv II – expressing wishes about unreal situations.
focus: 'ich wünschte' flags an unreal wish and pulls the subjunctive — könnte, not kann

target: Wenn es nach mir ginge, würden wir öfter gemeinsam verreisen.
english: If it were up to me, we would travel together more often.
old: 'ginge' – konjunktiv II of gehen (geht), softening this into a hypothetical or polite expression.
focus: 'wenn es nach mir ginge' = if it were up to me — a fixed subjunctive idiom, not a literal 'goes'

target: Wir verlassen uns bei diesem Projekt vollständig auf eure fachliche Expertise.
english: We completely rely on your professional expertise for this project.
old: 'sich verlassen auf' + acc. = to rely on.
focus: The real landmine: verlassen alone = to leave/abandon, but reflexive sich verlassen auf = to rely on. Quote 'verlassen uns ... auf' from the card and lead with that two-meanings flip, not just the gloss.

target: Immerhin hat er sich die Mühe gemacht, persönlich zu erscheinen.
english: At least he made the effort to appear in person.
old: 'Immerhin' – 'at least/after all' – concessive softener.
focus: immerhin flags a redeeming point – 'at least / still'. Drop the 'concessive softener' jargon; quote 'Immerhin hat er sich die Mühe gemacht' and make the consolation sense concrete.

target: Das ist ja wohl das Mindeste, was man erwarten kann.
english: That's surely the least one can expect.
old: 'Ja wohl' – emphatic agreement with a standard.
focus: In 'Das ist ja wohl das Mindeste', ja wohl adds an indignant 'surely/obviously' emphasis. Quote the card, plain words, drop the vague 'agreement with a standard'.

target: Das ist ja unglaublich, dass er die Prüfung bestanden hat!
english: That's incredible that he passed the exam!
old: Modal particle 'ja': expresses surprise or confirmation – 'well!/indeed!'
focus: Drop the 'modal particle' label. Plain words: 'ja' in 'Das ist ja unglaublich' flags the fact as evident/reacted-to emphasis, with no separate word in English.

target: Komm doch mal vorbei, wenn du in der Gegend bist.
english: Do come by when you're in the area.
old: Particle 'doch mal': softens request, makes it friendlier – 'why don't you'.
focus: Drop the 'Particle' lead. Hook = doch mal turns the bare command 'Komm vorbei' into a warm 'why don't you drop by' invitation.
